lesson.title: Gluing Text Together with the Plus Sign
lesson.summary: String concatenation uses the + operator to join two or more string values end to end into a single new string, and it only works when every operand is already a string.
lesson.body:
Concatenation is the operation of joining strings together to form a longer string. Python reuses the familiar + operator for this, but when both operands are strings instead of numbers, + means join rather than add. If first is "Ada" and last is "Lovelace", the expression first + " " + last builds a new string by placing the characters of each piece one after another: "Ada", then a single space character, then "Lovelace", producing "Ada Lovelace". Nothing about the original variables changes, since strings are immutable, so concatenation always produces a brand new string rather than modifying one in place.

Python is strict about types during concatenation, and that strictness trips up almost every beginner at least once. The expression "Score: " + 95 raises a TypeError, because Python refuses to silently guess whether you meant to combine text and a number. Unlike some languages that automatically convert a number to text when it meets a string, Python requires you to be explicit. The fix is to wrap the number in the built-in str() function first: "Score: " + str(95) correctly produces "Score: 95". This connects directly back to the String Type concept: a string is a distinct type from an integer or float, and + only concatenates when every operand on both sides is that same string type.

Trace a slightly larger example. Suppose city = "Boston" and state = "MA". The expression city + ", " + state builds the result in three sequential joins: first city + ", " produces "Boston, ", and then that result is joined with state to produce "Boston, MA". Python evaluates concatenation left to right, treating each intermediate result as a new complete string before the next + is applied.

This behavior is a deliberate design choice, not an oversight. Requiring an explicit str() conversion means a program never silently does the wrong thing when a number sneaks into a spot meant for text; the error surfaces immediately at the line that caused it, rather than producing a mysterious or subtly wrong string somewhere downstream. That predictability is worth the extra keystrokes.

Concatenation shows up constantly in real programs: building a full name from a first and last name, assembling a sentence of output from several pieces of data, or accumulating a longer string one small piece at a time inside a loop. More than two strings can be chained in one expression too, as in greeting + ", " + name + "!", which Python still evaluates left to right, joining the first two pieces into an intermediate string before joining that result with the next piece, and so on until one final string remains.

It is worth noticing that concatenation with + is different from the closely related operation covered next, string repetition with *, which builds a longer string out of one string repeated, rather than several different strings joined together. Both operations share the same underlying idea, that + and * mean something different for strings than they do for numbers, and both always produce a new string rather than changing an existing one.
